intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive pyridoxine-refractory sideroblastic anemia-2 (SIDBA2) is caused by mutation in the SLC25A38 gene.

checks.evidence_quote: we define a previously unknown form of autosomal recessive nonsyndromic congenital sideroblastic anemia, associated with mutations in the gene encoding the erythroid specific mitochondrial carrier family protein SLC25A38
checks.explanation: The abstract links autosomal recessive nonsyndromic congenital sideroblastic anemia to mutations in SLC25A38. It does not call the disease pyridoxine-refractory or use the name SIDBA2. Only the abstract was supplied.

paragraphs.text: Pyridoxine-refractory sideroblastic anemia-2 (SIDBA2) is an autosomal recessive nonsyndromic congenital sideroblastic anemia. The sideroblastic anemias are defined by ringed sideroblasts, which are bone marrow erythroid precursors with pathologic iron deposits within mitochondria (Guernsey et al., 2009). Affected individuals have had anemia from birth that did not respond to pyridoxine and needed transfusions (Jardine et al., 1994).

checks.evidence_quote: we define a previously unknown form of autosomal recessive nonsyndromic congenital sideroblastic anemia
checks.explanation: The abstract supports the description as autosomal recessive, nonsyndromic and congenital. It does not mention pyridoxine refractoriness.

checks.claim: The sideroblastic anemias are defined by ringed sideroblasts.

paragraphs.text: In a female infant with congenital refractory sideroblastic anemia, Manabe et al. (1982) found markedly reduced delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthetase activity in erythroblasts, both with and without pyridoxal phosphate. Erythroblast mitochondrial neutral protease activity was normal. This protease specifically inactivates the apo form of ALA synthetase, and the sensitivity of apo-ALA synthetase to the protease was also normal. The authors suggested that the reduced ALA synthetase activity resulted from impaired production of the enzyme rather than rapid destruction, which could explain why the patient did not respond to pyridoxine.

paragraphs.text: Jardine et al. (1994) concluded that the sideroblastic anemia in the family they studied was very likely an autosomal recessive trait. The affected brother and sister had unaffected parents and had inherited different maternal alleles at the ALAS2 locus. The mother showed random X inactivation in her peripheral leukocytes, indicating that she did not carry an X-linked sideroblastic anemia mutation. Guernsey et al. (2009) established autosomal recessive inheritance of this form of nonsyndromic congenital sideroblastic anemia.

paragraphs.text: Jardine et al. (1994) excluded the ALAS2 gene at Xp11.21 as the cause of disease in a family with pyridoxine-refractory sideroblastic anemia. Sequencing ALAS2 in the affected son found no mutation in the coding region, the intron/exon boundaries, or the 1-kb 5-prime promoter region. They found a G-to-A transition polymorphism 220 nucleotides 3-prime of the AATAAA polyadenylation signal and used it to follow inheritance of the locus. Using mismatch PCR followed by XmnI restriction analysis of 148 alleles, they estimated the frequency of this polymorphism at 25%. The 2 affected sibs had inherited different maternal ALAS2 alleles.

paragraphs.text: Using positional cloning, Guernsey et al. (2009) found that autosomal recessive nonsyndromic congenital sideroblastic anemia was associated with mutations in the SLC25A38 gene. SLC25A38 encodes an erythroid-specific mitochondrial carrier family protein. The authors showed that SLC25A38 is important for heme biosynthesis in eukaryotes.
